title: Hansen Site (15GP14)
summary: Near South Portsmouth in Greenup County, the Hansen Site is an Ohio River terrace with Late Archaic camps and later Woodland and Fort Ancient communities.
bodyMarkdown:
The Hansen Site (15Gp14) is an archaeological site in Greenup County, on a flood terrace of the Ohio River. It covers about 15 acres (6 hectares). Native people returned to this spot again and again over thousands of years, and their camps and houses left a layered record that archaeologists have studied.

The [Wikipedia article on the Hansen Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hansen_site) places it in the same stretch of valley as Lower Shawneetown and the Old Fort Earthworks, near where the Scioto River meets the Ohio. That makes it one of a cluster of important sites around the river mouth.

## Late Archaic summer camps

The earliest known use of the terrace dates to the Late Archaic period, around 2000 BCE. Archaeologists think people lived there lightly, probably during the summer months. They left distinctive projectile points of the Cave Run, Merom and Rowlette styles. Tests of material from the excavations returned uncalibrated dates of 2060 and 1930 BCE.

## Two Woodland villages

People came back during the Middle and Late Woodland periods, in two separate episodes. The first, from about 300 to 450 CE, was an intensive occupation centered on three circular buildings made with single posts, along with small clusters of households. Excavators found evidence of stone tool making, food storage and waste disposal.

The second episode, from about 500 to 600 CE, looked different. Life centered on more communal structures, and work such as tool making seems to have taken place in shared areas.

## The earthworks next door

The Hansen article says that during this time, people of the area's Adena culture built the nearby [Old Fort Earthworks](/stories/old-fort-earthworks-15gp1-greenup-county/) and the Biggs Site, both parts of the larger Portsmouth Earthworks complex. The [Wikipedia article on the Portsmouth Earthworks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth_Earthworks) gives a different time frame. It credits the complex to the Adena and Ohio Hopewell cultures between 100 BCE and 500 CE, which would place most of the building before Hansen's second village. Readers should treat the exact timing as unsettled.

That article describes the complex as three sections spread over twenty miles of the valley, crossing the river into Kentucky in several places. It was surveyed and mapped by E. G. Squier in 1847.

## Later visitors

The Hansen article says Fort Ancient people used the terrace after 600 CE. The [Wikipedia article on the Fort Ancient culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Ancient) dates that culture to about 1000–1750 CE. Both dates are shown here because the sources do not agree.

Centuries later, Shawnee, Iroquois and Delaware people built [Lower Shawneetown](/stories/lower-shawneetown-at-the-scioto-mouth/) nearby, a center of trade and diplomacy from about 1734 to 1758.

## Kentucky today

Most of what is known about the Hansen Site comes from chapters by Richard W. Jeffries and Darlene Applegate in The Archaeology of Kentucky: An Update, published by the Kentucky Heritage Council in 2008. The site is a record of Native life in Greenup County across thousands of years. Its buried remains are best left undisturbed.
